extracted.intended_audience: aspiring interactive-fiction writers and Choice of Games players/fans
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative notes for creating or judging Choice of Games-style interactive novels (ChoiceScript text games), emphasizing player agency, branching, worldbuilding, and use of ChoiceScript resources. Also a reader-facing guide to notable exemplary titles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Player agency / choices influence narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Interactive fiction allows the reader, or player, to interact with its narrative, influencing the course of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design choices so they actually alter the direction or outcome of the story rather than being superficial. The post emphasizes that interactive fiction is a cross between a game and a book because the player affects the course of events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role-playing / player as main character
rubrics_metrics.description: Interactive fiction tends to involve role-playing, with the reader/player taking the role of a main character in the story and making decisions that affect the characters and the outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write from the perspective of a player-character whose decisions shape relationships, events, and ending; support identification with that role through meaningful options and consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaningful long-term consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Each branch of magic comes with its own harmful long-term consequences down the road, so the player must carefully weigh the costs and benefits of each spell they perform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure choices have costs and benefits that ripple forward through the story so players must deliberate; avoid choices that only change minor text without substantive future impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Branching and replay value
rubrics_metrics.description: There are many possible branches in the second-to-last chapter of the story, which gives the game great replay value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide divergent branches and substantive different outcomes to encourage replaying; branching should feel significant rather than cosmetic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-rounded, interesting characters
rubrics_metrics.description: The characters are well-rounded and interesting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop NPCs and companions with depth and facets that react believably to player choices; strong characterization increases player investment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compelling themes and thought-provoking questions
rubrics_metrics.description: The game raises compelling questions about the hard choices oppressed communities must make in the face of injustice and violence; it's described as 'beautiful and thought-provoking' and explores the nature of art and our place in the universe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use interactive fiction to engage with substantial themes (morality, oppression, art, free will) — thematic depth can elevate a game from entertaining to memorable.

rubrics_metrics.name: World-building and cultural variety
rubrics_metrics.description: Interesting world-building, with a variety of cultures/peoples in the game-world and a diverse pantheon of animal gods; secondary-world fantasy settings are highlighted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create distinct cultures, religions, and settings that inform choices and character motivations; rich worldbuilding provides context for meaningful player decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Player customization and multiple playstyles
rubrics_metrics.description: The player can design their own robots, control appearance and functions, or become an athlete, a nerd, a popular kid, a theater geek, or a rebellious delinquent; can become a renowned filmmaker, paleontologist, physicist, or big-game hunter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer a variety of playstyles and roles so players can pursue different identities and goals; customization increases replayability and player ownership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre hybridity and cross-genre appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles are often hybrids (e.g., part tour guide simulator, part science fiction, part philosophical exploration, part romance; or hybrid murder mystery, political campaign simulator, and urban fantasy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mixing genres can create unique experiences that defy classification and attract varied audiences; don't be afraid to combine mechanics or themes from different genres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessible sampling / free first chapters
rubrics_metrics.description: All of these games/novels have first chapters that are free to play online, giving you a taste for their stories; some games are completely free to play all the way through online.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide free samples or demos (e.g., first chapter) so readers can try the game before purchasing; this helps discovery and builds audience trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear stats/attributes reflecting choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Your choices shape your dragon’s brutality, finesse, cunning, honor, disdain, vigilance, infamy, and wealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tracked attributes and visible consequences to make choices feel consequential and to enable mechanical variation between playthroughs; attributes should map sensibly to choices and outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity of playable species / character types
rubrics_metrics.description: You can play as any of more than ten moreau species, from a wolf, tiger, or bear to a capybara, each with its own strengths and weaknesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer a meaningful roster of playable character types or backgrounds that affect gameplay and narrative perspective; distinct options should lead to different experiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral and ethical dilemma design
rubrics_metrics.description: Games raise interesting questions about morality, religion, and free will and force players to weigh costs, benefits, and difficult choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design dilemmas where there is no obviously 'right' answer and where choices illuminate character and theme; let consequences probe ethical complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ChoiceScript resources and community
rubrics_metrics.description: Resources for creating ChoiceScript games/interactive fiction: Choice of Games' make-your-own-games/choicescript-intro, ChoiceScript Wiki, and the Choice of Games forum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For producing ChoiceScript games, consult official ChoiceScript documentation, community wiki, and forums for technical guidance, examples, and peer support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entertainment value / fun writing moments
rubrics_metrics.description: Games are described as 'really cool', 'good stuff', 'great', 'neat and entertaining', and 'a nifty furry game'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sprinkle humor, surprising moments, and well-placed setpieces to keep the experience enjoyable; tone and voice matter for player enjoyment.
